unique_advisories.description: Use After Free vulnerability in Apache Arrow C++.  This issue affects Apache Arrow C++ from 15.0.0 through 23.0.0. It can be triggered when reading an Arrow IPC file (but not an IPC stream) with pre-buffering enabled, if the IPC file contains data with variadic buffers (such as Binary View and String View data). Depending on the number of variadic buffers in a record batch column and on the temporal sequence of multi-threaded IO, a write to a dangling pointer could occur. The value (a `std::shared_ptr<Buffer>` object) that is written to the dangling pointer is not under direct control of the attacker.  Pre-buffering is disabled by default but can be enabled using a specific C++ API call (`RecordBatchFileReader::PreBufferMetadata`). The functionality is not exposed in language bindings (Python, Ruby, C GLib), so these bindings are not vulnerable.  The most likely consequence of this issue would be random crashes or memory corruption when reading specific kinds of IPC files. If the application allows ingesting IPC files from untrusted sources, this could plausibly be exploited for denial of service. Inducing more targeted kinds of misbehavior (such as confidential data extraction from the running process) depends on memory allocation and multi-threaded IO temporal patterns that are unlikely to be easily controlled by an attacker.  Advice for users of Arrow C++:  1. check whether you enable pre-buffering on the IPC file reader (using `RecordBatchFileReader::PreBufferMetadata`)   2. if so, either disable pre-buffering (which may have adverse performance consequences), or switch to Arrow 23.0.1 which is not vulnerable

dispositions.B301/B403: Five pickle loads and two imports implement private single/parallel worker transfers. Parent-created TemporaryDirectory paths, validated recording identifiers and parent-owned queues constrain paths. User-selected pickle is a separate explicit-trust operation in core.load_sensor_file. These findings rely on trusted code and OS protection of the account/temporary files; executable deserialization remains a trust boundary.
dispositions.B404/B603: Developer/build scripts execute explicit argument lists without shell=True. Commands are Python, build/check tooling, PowerShell signature inventory and SDK SignTool. Recording contents do not choose executables or command text.
dispositions.B607: git and pwsh resolve through PATH in developer/build/signing tooling; safe use requires a trusted executable search path.

threat_model: Local desktop application running with the launching user permissions; no privilege separation from that account.
Recordings and result files can be malformed. Explicitly accepted pickle inputs, classifier models, application code and the toolchain must be trusted.
Run history and its output paths are trusted local metadata; there is no application-level cryptographic integrity or access policy.
Worker isolation supports cancellation and responsiveness; it is not a security sandbox.

manual_review.assessment: Untrusted pickle is rejected before the official loader; GUI trust defaults to No. JSON result reopening reconstructs tables without unpickling or automatically loading sources. TSDF scale factors/channel identities are validated. Native parsers and all third-party source were not exhaustively audited or fuzz-tested.

Same-filesystem temporary writes replace destinations only after completion. Known sources, recognized TSDF time/value companions, hard/symbolic aliases and local saved-run destinations are protected. CSV formula-like strings and headers are prefixed. Deletion requires confirmation, defaults to Cancel, and protects directories and files referenced by retained runs. Path checks do not authenticate history or harden against an adversarial same-account filesystem.

Complete derived results, metadata, paths and logs persist in plaintext under the user data location, with legacy fallback. Original recordings are not copied into saved runs. No app encryption, login, role policy or cryptographic integrity check. Separate OS accounts, ACLs and drive encryption are deployment controls, not application guarantees.

Job/UI/toolbox error boundaries preserve full tracebacks, including process forwarding; notices and structured counts stay concise. Logs may contain filenames, absolute paths, recording/subject identifiers and diagnostic values. No automatic redaction; share logs as potentially sensitive data.

Single recordings use one worker; independent recordings use up to two with CPU/RAM estimates. The parent owns processes/private transfer paths, bounds dispatched work and cleans on Stop/failure/completion. Estimates are not resource caps. Abrupt parent/system termination can leave temporary data or surviving workers; deletion is not secure erasure.

No automatic recording upload, telemetry, elevation or service/registry installation implementation found in the wrapper. Explicit documentation links open a browser. Network isolation and every dependency runtime behavior were not instrumented.

Direct runtime versions, Open Movement revision and Actions commits are pinned; transitive/build-backend dependencies are not fully hash-locked. Build/signing checkouts disable persisted credentials. Tag-only publication/status jobs have contents:write; status checkout credentials push refs/notes/paradigma-releases. Only environment-gated signing has id-token:write; application execution occurs in a separate verification job. Release checks verify tag/version/source, complete inventory, no symlinks and uploaded sizes/digests before publication. These are reviewed/tested controls, not verification of a current binary or actual publisher signature.
